title: Dunes
escapeBrief: To get out you worked out when to set off to haul the condenser back from the stranded water steamer. It is 1928; the river has not flooded in two years, the company has abandoned the town and stopped the water shipments, and its last steamer, carrying a sea-water condenser, lies beyond a breach the storm cut through the sand spit. The town's tanks last 70 days, to 17 December. Hauling the condenser across the bar at the mouth of the breach takes three days of dry bar, and nobody can wait on the shore, so you needed the date. The engineer built a tide machine to predict the water over the bar, and a storm scattered its four pulleys. You found them in the general store, on the cliff winch, in the dunes and on the flats, and fitted them to the machine's four shafts: the moon's month, the season, the moon's near-and-far, and the afternoon wind. A bigger pulley swings the wire further, so which pulley goes on which shaft says how much each rhythm moves the water. The lore told you the moon pulls hardest and that its near-and-far pulls less than the sun, which left three ways to fit them; cranking back to the dates in the engineer's logbook showed which one puts the pen where he measured the water. Cranking forward, the bar stays under the wading line for three days only once before the water runs out, from the evening of 7 December, so you set off on 7, 8 or 9 December. The old hands' rule, go at the dark-moon spring, uses the moon alone, and on 12 October it sends you into two metres of water. Adding several rhythms, each weighted by how much it matters, checking the result against what was measured, and beating a one-input rule is exactly what a multiple regression does, on the machine or in R.
